evidence.text: Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evaluated using Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment using Uni-G and comparison against expert-validated diagnostic labels. Results: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. A deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications, including 639 without numeric checks, while preserving 268 of 269 applications independently supported by Uni-G. Restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%. Under matched instructions and an identical output schema, retrieval increased unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained unchanged at 62.6%. Conclusion: These findings identify a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation: retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence. Measurement-based verification can reduce unsupported criterion applications, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

evidence.text: RAG-TRACE establishes a measurement-centered approach to assessing evidence reliability in AI-generated ECG reports. The evaluation highlights the importance of distinguishing retrieved clinical information from criteria supported by patient-specific measurements. Its verification mechanism provides a transparent means of identifying unsupported applications while preserving valid quantitative evidence. Importantly, criterion-level reliability and diagnostic completeness represent separate dimensions of report quality that require independent assessment. Integrating these principles into clinical RAG pipelines could support more interpretable and auditable AI-generated reports. Future work should extend RAG-TRACE to broader clinical datasets, incorporate measurement-aware retrieval, and evaluate its impact through clinician-adjudicated assessments.

A retrieved criterion may be clinically relevant without being satisfied by the patient’s measurements. Other retrieved information, such as calibration settings or laboratory values, may lack a corresponding ECG measurement. These limitations create a critical gap between retrieval relevance and verifiable diagnostic evidence. Structured reports are generated with and without retrieval. A deterministic rule evaluates applied criteria against Marquette 12SL measurements, while Uni-G provides independent assessment. Diagnostic agreement and completeness are evaluated separately against expert-validated labels. Additional experiments assess retrieval constraints, controlled generation settings, and generalizability to other physiological recordings

evidence.text: Retrieval-augmented ECG reporting exposes a gap between clinical relevance and patient-specific evidence. Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1 mini reports, with 639 of 647 withdrawn applications lacking numeric checks. Qwen3-8B exhibited a distinct failure pattern, with 203 of 211 measurement-disconfirmed applications independently rejected by Uni-G. The differences highlight two sources of unreliable reporting: unverifiable retrieved content and incorrect application of measurable criteria. The deliberately constructed criteria library increased exposure to these failures, limiting generalization to routine clinical practice. RAG-TRACE complements research on retrieval robustness, medical citation reliability, and multi-step clinical reasoning Park and Lee (2024) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Wind et al. (2025) by assessing retrieved evidence against patient-specific measurements. Verification preserved 268 of 269 independently supported GPT-4.1 mini applications and 274 of 282 Qwen3-8B applications. This selective withdrawal offers that unsupported criteria can be removed with limited loss of measurement-supported claims. The zero release score reflects the deterministic rule itself, making independent measurement agreement essential for assessing verification performance. Controlled comparisons further distinguish retrieval effects from changes in diagnostic scoring. Under identical instructions and output schemas, unsupported-criterion reports increased from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained at 62.6%. The different-schema comparison showed a modest decrease in micro-F1 (0.804 to 0.795) and scored hypertrophy recall (0.617 to 0.514)

evidence.text: The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is an essential diagnostic tool for assessing cardiac activity through measurable intervals, axes, and voltages Kligfield et al. (2007) ; Mason et al. (2007) . Large datasets such as PTB-XL, comprising 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients Wagner et al. (2020) , have advanced automated ECG interpretation Strodthoff et al. (2021) . Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in detecting cardiac abnormalities Ribeiro et al. (2020) ; Hannun et al. (2019) ; Alday et al. (2020) ; Mehari and Strodthoff (2022) and supporting cardiovascular screening Attia et al. (2019) ; Siontis et al. (2021) . Nevertheless, generating reliable clinical reports requires more than diagnostic predictions. Each reported finding must be supported by patient-specific evidence. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential for generating clinical narratives Tu et al. (2025) and diagnostic explanations Singhal et al. (2023) ; Nori et al. (2023) . Their outputs can contain unsupported statements and inaccurate evidence attribution Ji et al. (2023) ; Maynez et al. (2020) . Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates external knowledge to improve factual grounding Lewis et al. (2020) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Shuster et al. (2021) , with promising applications in medical question answering Xiong et al. (2024) ; Zakka et al. (2024) and clinical information extraction Agrawal et al. (2022) . Recent studies have investigated evidence alignment in clinical question answering Irankhah and Fodeh (2026) and query-level reliability in retriever upgrades Irankhah and Arif (2026) . These advances highlight the importance of evidence quality, but the reliability of retrieved criteria in ECG report generation remains insufficiently examined

RAG-TRACE: Tracing Measurement Evidence and Diagnostic Completeness in AI-Generated ECG Reports | Introduction

The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is an essential diagnostic tool for assessing cardiac activity through measurable intervals, axes, and voltages Kligfield et al. (2007) ; Mason et al. (2007) . Large datasets such as PTB-XL, comprising 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients Wagner et al. (2020) , have advanced automated ECG interpretation Strodthoff et al. (2021) . Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in detecting cardiac abnormalities Ribeiro et al. (2020) ; Hannun et al. (2019) ; Alday et al. (2020) ; Mehari and Strodthoff (2022) and supporting cardiovascular screening Attia et al. (2019) ; Siontis et al. (2021) . Nevertheless, generating reliable clinical reports requires more than diagnostic predictions. Each reported finding must be supported by patient-specific evidence. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential for generating clinical narratives Tu et al. (2025) and diagnostic explanations Singhal et al. (2023) ; Nori et al. (2023) . Their outputs can contain unsupported statements and inaccurate evidence attribution Ji et al. (2023) ; Maynez et al. (2020) . Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates external knowledge to improve factual grounding Lewis et al. (2020) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Shuster et al. (2021) , with promising applications in medical question answering Xiong et al. (2024) ; Zakka et al. (2024) and clinical information extraction Agrawal et al. (2022) . Recent studies have investigated evidence alignment in clinical question answering Irankhah and Fodeh (2026) and query-level reliability in retriever upgrades Irankhah and Arif (2026) . These advances highlight the importance of evidence quality, but the reliability of retrieved criteria in ECG report generation remains insufficiently examined

Table 1 summarizes the library. Composition of the ECG criteria library. Each numeric threshold is an operational predicate used for verification. It is not sufficient, by itself, for a clinical diagnosis. Following construction of the criteria library, three retrieval strategies were evaluated: keyword overlap, term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF), and Okapi BM25. Retrieval queries were constructed from the names of diagnostic superclasses with calibrated probabilities \geq 0.5 , without access to held-out diagnostic labels. For keyword retrieval, the relevance score between query q and criterion card c was defined as  where T(q) and T(c) denote their respective token sets. Ties were resolved using card identifiers. TF–IDF and BM25 operated on the same queries and criterion descriptions, with BM25 parameters k_{1}=1.5 and b=0.75 . Each strategy retrieved the three highest-ranked cards. BM25 was evaluated using saved queries without generating additional reports, and biomedical embedding-based retrieval was not included. Figure 1 illustrates the overall RAG-TRACE pipeline, from dataset preparation and criteria library construction to evidence retrieval and structured ECG report generation. Overview of the RAG-TRACE framework, showing dataset preparation, ECG criteria library construction, evidence retrieval strategies, and structured inputs for language model-based ECG report generation.

evidence.text: All 1,083 GPT-4.1-mini patients and 1,082 Qwen3-8B patients had parseable reports across the three retrieval conditions. For GPT-4.1-mini, the prespecified cue-based expert-absent diagnosis rate increased from 7.5% without retrieval to 10.1% with keyword retrieval (paired difference 0.026, 95% CI 0.006–0.045; McNemar p=0.008 ). TF–IDF produced a rate of 11.0%. This cue-based metric misses some affirmative statements, as examined in Section 3.8 . Keyword retrieval produced untestable or 12SL-disconfirmed criterion applications in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. Each report contained an average of 0.891 applied criteria: 0.590 lacked numeric checks, 0.007 failed 12SL predicates, and 0.294 were supported. The release score became zero after deterministic withdrawal by definition; independent Uni-G and expert-label results remained separate (Table 3 ). At least one top-three card lacked a numeric check in 81.4% of keyword queries, 79.8% of BM25 queries, and 73.6% of TF–IDF queries. Keyword retrieval and the same note after the 12SL withdrawal. Expert diagnosis absent: an affirmed superclass is missing from the PTB-XL label. Uni-G rejects: an applied criterion fails the second algorithm. Release: an applied card has no check, or the 12SL predicate is false. The last row is a mean count, not a record rate.

evidence.text: . Affirmed diagnoses were extracted using the prespecified cue-based rule and, separately, the exploratory label-aware approach. Since verification modifies only criterion applications, diagnostic consistency remains unchanged after withdrawal. An additional statement-level metric assessed discrepancies between the original eight criteria and their linked cardiologist statement codes, including unsupported applications and omitted findings. Diagnostic agreement was quantified using micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 across the five superclasses. Class-specific recall was calculated among patients with the corresponding reference diagnosis, while patient-level recall measured the proportion of reference superclasses identified in each report. Paired effects were expressed as \Delta=\theta_{\mathrm{key}}-\theta_{\mathrm{none}} , comparing keyword retrieval with no retrieval on the same patients. Confidence intervals were obtained from 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

evidence.text: Three complementary metrics were used to assess criterion applicability, independent measurement agreement, and diagnostic consistency with expert-validated labels. For record i , let A_{i} denote the set of applied criteria, x_{i} the corresponding measurements, and \kappa(c) the numeric verification rule associated with criterion c . The predicates P_{12} and P_{U} represent Marquette 12SL and Uni-G evaluations, respectively. Let G_{i}=\{k:y_{i,k}=1\} denote the reference diagnostic superclasses and D_{i} the affirmed superclasses extracted from the generated report. The record-level indicators were defined as  The corresponding rates were calculated as the mean of each indicator across records. The release score ( r_{i} ) identifies untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criterion applications. Deterministic 12SL withdrawal sets this score to zero by construction, while the Uni-G score ( u_{i} ) provides an independent assessment. The agreement-based configuration requires both measurement predicates to hold and consequently sets u_{i}=0 by construction. Withdrawals were categorized by missing numeric checks or failed 12SL predicates, with the latter further classified according to Uni-G agreement. Low-probability diagnostic assertions, defined by calibrated probabilities below 0.5, were evaluated separately. The earlier combined rate represents their union with release-score violations. Diagnostic consistency ( e_{i} ) identifies reports affirming at least one superclass absent from the reference labels. Affirmed diagnoses were extracted using the prespecified cue-based rule and, separately, the exploratory label-aware approach. Since verification modifies only criterion applications, diagnostic consistency remains unchanged after withdrawal

evidence.text: For the eight criteria linked to cardiologist statement codes, keyword retrieval increased statement mismatch from 7.5% to 24.9% for GPT-4.1 mini and from 1.6% to 34.1% for Qwen3-8B. The two-algorithm agreement rule reduced these rates to 22.2% and 19.6%, respectively, without a substantial increase in unstated linked findings (Table 5 ). Among retained applications, the linked code was present in 27.5% of 204 GPT-4.1 mini applications and 12.8% of 218 Qwen3-8B applications. Numeric support and diagnostic-label agreement therefore remained distinct. Statement mismatch against stored cardiologist codes for the original eight checks, and the mean number of those findings left unstated.

evidence.text: We developed a novel LLM constellation architecture, namely Polaris  with multiple specialized healthcare LLMs working in unison for real-time patient-AI voice conversations. Our architecture allowed for a primary agent to adopt a human-like conversational approach, exhibiting empathy and building rapport and trust; whereas the specialist agents were optimized for specific healthcare related tasks. We found this architecture allowed for accurate medical reasoning, fact-checking, and the avoidance of hallucinations, while maintaining a natural conversation with patients. We performed extensive phase one and phase two testing of our system with U.S-licensed nurses and U.S.-licensed physicians. Impressively, on subjective criteria, our study participants rated our AI agent on par with U.S.-licensed nurses on multiple dimensions. On objective criteria, our medium-size AI agents significantly outperformed much larger general-purpose LLMs like GPT-4 in medical accuracy and safety. We are now moving to phase three testing, which requires much more extensive evaluation to be completed by several thousands of licensed nurses and licensed physicians, as well as by our health system and digital health partners. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to conduct such an extensive safety assessment of any Generative AI technology for real-life healthcare deployment. In conclusion, we foresee a promising future for AI agents to improve healthcare by filling a large portion of the staffing gap. As we continue to push the boundaries and overcome challenges, our goal remains to provide scalable and safe systems that alleviate the burden on human health care providers and improve patient satisfaction, health care access, and health outcomes.

We are now moving to phase three testing, which requires much more extensive evaluation to be completed by several thousands of licensed nurses and licensed physicians, as well as by our health system and digital health partners. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to conduct such an extensive safety assessment of any Generative AI technology for real-life healthcare deployment. In conclusion, we foresee a promising future for AI agents to improve healthcare by filling a large portion of the staffing gap. As we continue to push the boundaries and overcome challenges, our goal remains to provide scalable and safe systems that alleviate the burden on human health care providers and improve patient satisfaction, health care access, and health outcomes.

searches.query: A medical-device client wants to add retrieval to its AI ECG reporting tool. What did the RAG-TRACE study evaluate, what did retrieval do to unsupported criteria and to diagnostic recall, how well did deterministic verification work, and what limits apply before deployment?
